subtopics.title: Why Equations Must Balance — Conservation of Mass

questions.question: The law of conservation of mass states that in a chemical reaction:
options: Mass slowly turns into energy
Atoms are neither created nor destroyed — they are only rearranged
Heavy atoms break into lighter ones
The products always weigh less than the reactants

questions.question: In the unbalanced line C3H8 + O2 gives CO2 + H2O, the census shows:
options: Both sides already tally
Only hydrogen fails to tally
Two carbons and six hydrogens missing on the right, one oxygen invented
Too many carbons on the right

questions.question: Balancing an equation means adjusting:
options: How many of each molecule takes part — never what the molecules are
The formulas of the products until they fit
The temperature of the reaction
The direction of the arrow

subtopics.title: The One Commandment — Coefficients, Never Subscripts

questions.question: The one commandment of balancing is:
options: Balance oxygen before anything else
Always double every coefficient
Change subscripts freely but never coefficients
Change only coefficients — never edit a subscript

questions.question: Editing H2O into H2O2 to make an equation balance is illegal because:
options: Subscripts may only be doubled, never increased by one
It changes the substance's identity — hydrogen peroxide is a different chemical from water
Peroxide is too dangerous to write down
The equation would have too many atoms

questions.question: Four H2O contains in total:
options: Eight hydrogens and four oxygens — the coefficient multiplies every atom in the formula
Four hydrogens and four oxygens
Two hydrogens and one oxygen
Eight hydrogens and eight oxygens

questions.question: In combustion equations oxygen is balanced last because:
options: Oxygen atoms are the heaviest involved
Oxygen is a gas and gases go last
It appears in both products and stands alone as O2 — its count depends on everything else
Oxygen never needs a coefficient

subtopics.title: Balancing the Propane Equation — C, then H, then O

questions.question: Carbon settles first with coefficient three because:
options: Oxygen arrives in pairs
Carbon is the lightest element in the equation
Three is always the first coefficient tried
Propane carries three carbons and each CO2 holds exactly one

questions.question: The oxygen step counts the right side first because:
options: That is where the demand sits — six oxygens in the carbon dioxides plus four in the waters, ten in all
The right side has fewer molecules
Oxygen only exists on the right
The left side cannot be counted

questions.question: The balanced propane equation, fully audited, is:
options: C3H8 + 3 O2 gives 3 CO2 + 4 H2O
C3H8 + 5 O2 gives 3 CO2 + 4 H2O — carbons three and three, hydrogens eight and eight, oxygens ten and ten
C3H8 + 5 O2 gives 4 CO2 + 3 H2O
2 C3H8 + 5 O2 gives 3 CO2 + 4 H2O

subtopics.title: Fractions, Final Form, and the Road to Stoichiometry

questions.question: Balancing butane, C4H10, the oxygen demand is thirteen atoms — thirteen halves of O2. The lawful fix is:
options: Leave thirteen over two as the final coefficient
Round thirteen halves up to seven
Double every coefficient: 2 C4H10 + 13 O2 gives 8 CO2 + 10 H2O
Change O2 to O so the count is whole

questions.question: The line 4 H2 + 2 O2 gives 4 H2O audits perfectly but is unfinished because:
options: Every coefficient divides by two — the final form is 2 H2 + O2 gives 2 H2O
Water needs a subscript change
Hydrogen cannot carry a coefficient of four
The audit only works for carbon compounds

questions.question: Exhibit two of the error museum — the audit-killer — is:
options: Balancing carbon before hydrogen
Writing the arrow backwards
Using whole numbers instead of fractions
Reading three CO2 as three carbons and two oxygens instead of three carbons and six oxygens

questions.question: Next term the coefficients one, five, three, four of the propane equation become:
options: Subscripts in bigger formulae
Mole ratios — one mole of propane consumes five of oxygen and delivers three of carbon dioxide and four of water
Percentages of the total mass
Volumes in litres at any conditions

subtopics.title: Nothing Goes Missing at the Braai

questions.question: Weighing everything that enters the braai flame and everything that leaves shows:
options: The flame destroys a little matter each second
Only the ash can be weighed
The two piles weigh exactly the same — atoms are rebuilt, never burned away
The gases weigh nothing

questions.question: In the flame, propane's carbons and hydrogens end up:
options: Destroyed by the heat
Carbons in carbon dioxide, hydrogens in water vapour — every atom delivered
Trapped in the cylinder
Converted into oxygen

questions.question: When the two sides of a written equation refuse to tally, the fault lies with:
options: Our counting — chemistry itself never loses atoms
The law of conservation of mass
The reaction being too fast
The arrow pointing the wrong way

questions.question: The courier picture of conservation of mass says:
options: Parcels may be lost if insured
Small parcels do not count
Extra parcels may arrive uninvited
Everything collected must be delivered — no parcel lost, none invented

subtopics.title: Buy More Packets, Don't Repack Them

questions.question: In the shopping picture, the coefficient is:
options: The number of packets bought — freely changeable, the contents untouched
The number of atoms inside one packet
The label on the packet
The price of the packet

questions.question: The subscript is locked because it is:
options: Too small to read reliably
Part of the label — change it and the product becomes a different substance
Always equal to the coefficient
Only used for gases

questions.question: Five O2 puts in your trolley:
options: Five oxygen atoms
Two oxygen atoms
Ten oxygen atoms — five packets of two
Seven oxygen atoms

questions.question: A formula with no number written in front of it:
options: Cannot take part in the reaction
Counts as zero molecules
Must be balanced first
Carries an invisible coefficient of one

subtopics.title: Easy Ones First, Then the Awkward One

questions.question: Carbon and hydrogen are the easy ones because:
options: They are lighter than oxygen
Each has exactly one destination — carbon dioxide or water — so each settles in a single move
They always take the coefficient one
They appear on both sides already balanced

questions.question: Packing oxygen first leads to:
options: A faster solution
Smaller coefficients
A balanced equation with fractions only
The loop — every later change breaks the oxygen count again

questions.question: Rebuilt from scratch, the propane numbers are:
options: One propane, five oxygen, three carbon dioxide, four water — and the audit gives three matches
One propane, three oxygen, three carbon dioxide, four water
Two propane, ten oxygen, six carbon dioxide, eight water as the final form
One propane, five oxygen, four carbon dioxide, three water

questions.question: Butane's six and a half pairs of oxygen are handled by:
options: Buying half a packet of oxygen
Rounding six and a half up to seven
Doubling the whole shopping list — two butane, thirteen oxygen, eight carbon dioxide, ten water
Ignoring the odd atom
